title: Ὄφις καὶ καρκίνος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 290. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄφις καὶ καρκίνος ἐν ταὐτῷ διέτριβον.
sentences.tr: Ophis kai karkinos en tautōi dietribon.
sentences.l: A snake and a crab were passing their time in the same place.
sentences.n: ἐν ταὐτῷ is crasis, the two words ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ run together; the mark over the alpha is the coronis of crasis, not a breathing.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ μὲν καρκίνος ἁπλῶς τῷ ὄφει καὶ εὐνοϊκῶς προσεφέρετο· ὁ δὲ ἀεὶ ὕπουλός τε καὶ πονηρὸς ἦν.
sentences.tr: Kai ho men karkinos haplōs tōi ophei kai eunoikōs prosephereto· ho de aei hypoulos te kai ponēros ēn.
sentences.l: And the crab on his side bore himself toward the snake simply and with goodwill; but the other was always festering-underneath and wicked.
sentences.i: The crab for his part dealt with the snake straightforwardly and with goodwill; the snake was always sly and malicious.
sentences.n: μέν … δέ sets the two characters against each other. ἁπλῶς is the fable's key word — single, unfolded, with nothing doubled over — and it will come back in ἐξαπλοῦσθαι and in ἁπλοῦν at the end. ὕπουλος is a wound healed over on the surface and still suppurating beneath.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ καρκίνου συνεχῶς αὐτῷ παραινοῦντος ἐξαπλοῦσθαι τὰ πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ διάθεσιν μιμεῖσθαι, ἐκεῖνος οὐκ ἐπείθετο.
sentences.tr: Tou de karkinou synechōs autōi parainountos exaplousthai ta pros auton kai tēn autou diathesin mimeisthai, ekeinos ouk epeitheto.
sentences.l: And the crab continually urging him to unfold his dealings toward him and to imitate the crab's own disposition, that one was not persuaded.
sentences.i: Though the crab kept urging him to be open in his dealings with him and to take on the crab's own disposition, the snake would not be persuaded.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute (τοῦ καρκίνου … παραινοῦντος) holds the crab's urging while the main clause reports the snake's refusal. ἐξαπλόω is to unfold, to spread out flat — the opposite of the coiled and the concealed, and a syllable away from ἁπλῶς. τὰ πρὸς αὐτόν, 'the things toward him', is his whole conduct in the friendship; τὴν αὐτοῦ διάθεσιν is the crab's disposition, not the snake's, though both pronouns are the same αὐτ- stem.

sentences.t: Διόπερ ἀγανακτήσας, παρατηρησάμενος αὐτὸν κοιμώμενον, τοῦ φάρυγγος ἐπιλαβόμενος ἀνεῖλε καὶ ἰδὼν αὐτὸν ἐκτεταμένον, εἶπεν· « Ὦ οὗτος, οὐ νῦν σε ἐχρῆν ἁπλοῦν εἶναι, ὅτε τέθνηκας, ὅτε δέ σοι παρῄνουν· καὶ οὐκ ⟨ἂν⟩ ἀνῄρησο. »
sentences.tr: Dioper aganaktēsas, paratērēsamenos auton koimōmenon, tou pharyngos epilabomenos aneile kai idōn auton ektetamenon, eipen· « Ō houtos, ou nyn se echrēn haploun einai, hote tethnēkas, hote de soi parēinoun· kai ouk ⟨an⟩ anēirēso. »
sentences.l: Therefore, having grown indignant, having watched for him asleep, having laid hold of his throat, he made away with him; and having seen him stretched out, he said: « You there, it was not now that you ought to be straight, when you are dead, but then, when I was advising you; and you ⟨would⟩ not have been made away with. »
sentences.i: So in indignation he watched until the snake was asleep, took him by the throat and killed him; and seeing him stretched out straight, he said: « You there — now is no time to be straight, now you are dead; the time was when I was advising you, and then you would not have been killed. »
sentences.n: ἐπιλαμβάνομαι takes the genitive of the part seized. The rebuke has the shape met at fable 134 and fable 75: not now, when it is of no use, but then, when it would have served; ἐχρῆν is the imperfect of obligation, of a duty that went unmet. Its point is in ἁπλοῦν, the ἁπλῶς of the opening line come back — the snake is straight at last, stretched out dead, the only straightness he ever managed. ⟨ἂν⟩ is Chambry's supplement, and without it the pluperfect ἀνῄρησο would state a fact rather than the contrary-to-fact 'you would not have been killed'. Ὦ οὗτος is blunt address, 'you there'.

sentences.t: Οὗτος ὁ λόγος εἰκότως ἂν λέγοιτο ἐπ’ ἐκείνων τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἳ παρὰ τὸν ἑαυτῶν βίον εἰς τοὺς φίλους πονηρευόμενοι μετὰ τὸν θάνατον εὐεργεσίας κατατίθενται.
sentences.tr: Houtos ho logos eikotōs an legoito ep’ ekeinōn tōn anthrōpōn hoi para ton heautōn bion eis tous philous ponēreuomenoi meta ton thanaton euergesias katatithentai.
sentences.l: This story might with good reason be spoken of those men who, dealing wickedly toward their friends throughout their own life, after death lay up benefactions.
sentences.i: This story might fairly be told of men who wrong their friends all their lives long, and only when death has come confer any benefit on them.
sentences.n: A closing formula of its own shape, beside the commoner οὗτος ὁ λόγος ἁρμόττει πρός (as at fable 41); ἂν λέγοιτο is the potential optative, the guarded 'might well be said'. κατατίθεμαι in the middle is to lay a thing down to one's own account, to put a benefit on deposit and so earn a claim on gratitude. μετὰ τὸν θάνατον is left unspecified, but παρὰ τὸν ἑαυτῶν βίον standing just before it points to the man's own death — a legacy, as the snake's one straight act was his corpse.
